Literary criticism:  
Bashō’s juxtaposition of the vivid, spatially dispersed plum blossoms against the walker’s ostensibly aimless motion creates an understated tension between external abundance and inner directionlessness. The seasonal image anchors the poem in a precise moment of early spring, while the temporal refrain flattens yesterday and today into a single, unbroken present. This flattening, coupled with the blossoms’ far-and-near placement, evokes a landscape that offers orientation without demanding a destination; the walker is free to drift precisely because the world itself is already fully arranged. The result is a quiet affirmation of wandering as its own form of fidelity to the season—motion without agenda becomes a way of inhabiting time rather than merely passing through it.

The poem presents the figure of a mature bridegroom whose fan, raised in greeting or conversation, momentarily blocks the view through the skylight above. The gesture is at once polite and intimate, suggesting that his very presence fills the room so completely that even a shaft of daylight is eclipsed by the sweep of his fan.

Bashō-era haikai often measured human worth by the quiet authority a person exerted over ordinary space. Here the skylight—an aperture that ordinarily admits the vastness of sky—is reduced to a mere backdrop for the bridegroom’s fan. The juxtaposition of “fifty” (an age when vigor might be expected to wane) with “new son-in-law” (a role charged with fresh social consequence) underscores a vitality that needs no youthful display; a single, graceful motion suffices to reorder the room’s light. The economy of the verse—three concrete images arranged without commentary—allows the reader to experience that reordering directly: the fan’s arc becomes, for an instant, the new horizon, and admiration arises not from stated praise but from the felt displacement of daylight itself.
